claim: The basolateral amygdala complex (BLA) is involved in a diverse array of functional roles.
source: The basolateral amygdala complex (BLA), extensively connected with both local amygdalar nuclei as well as long-range circuits, is involved in a diverse array of functional roles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of the BLA, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified both discrete and graded continuous gene-expression differences within the mouse BLA.
source: Here, beginning with single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified both discrete and graded continuous gene-expression differences within the mouse BLA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2-5.

claim: Discrete transcriptomic heterogeneity maps onto a sharp spatial border between the basal and lateral amygdala nuclei.
source: Via in situ hybridization, we next mapped this discrete transcriptomic heterogeneity onto a sharp spatial border between the basal and lateral amygdala nuclei, and identified continuous spatial gene-expression gradients within each of these regions.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Continuous spatial gene-expression gradients exist within the basal and lateral amygdala nuclei.
source: Via in situ hybridization, we next mapped this discrete transcriptomic heterogeneity onto a sharp spatial border between the basal and lateral amygdala nuclei, and identified continuous spatial gene-expression gradients within each of these regions.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Discrete and continuous spatial transformations of transcriptomic cell-type identity are recapitulated by local morphology.
source: These discrete and continuous spatial transformations of transcriptomic cell-type identity were recapitulated by local morphology as well as long-range connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Discrete and continuous spatial transformations of transcriptomic cell-type identity are recapitulated by long-range connectivity.
source: These discrete and continuous spatial transformations of transcriptomic cell-type identity were recapitulated by local morphology as well as long-range connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data presented in Figure 7.

claim: BLA excitatory neurons are a highly heterogeneous collection of neurons that spatially covary in molecular, cellular, and circuit properties.
source: Thus, BLA excitatory neurons are a highly heterogenous collection of neurons that spatially covary in molecular, cellular, and circuit properties.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the combined data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BLA heterogeneity likely drives pronounced spatial variation in BLA computation and function.
source: This heterogeneity likely drives pronounced spatial variation in BLA computation and function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The amygdala plays a role in acquisition and expression of conditioned fear memory.
source: Classically, the amygdala has been studied for the role it plays in acquisition and expression of conditioned fear memory (Fanselow and LeDoux, 1999; Maren and Quirk, 2004), with more recent evidence also implicating this brain region to be involved in other aversive states like anxiety (Daviu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The amygdala is involved in aversive states like anxiety.
source: Classically, the amygdala has been studied for the role it plays in acquisition and expression of conditioned fear memory (Fanselow and LeDoux, 1999; Maren and Quirk, 2004), with more recent evidence also implicating this brain region to be involved in other aversive states like anxiety (Daviu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The amygdala participates in appetitive and reward-based behavior.
source: Complementing this work examining the role of the amygdala in negative valence settings, it is also becoming increasingly apparent that the amygdala participates in appetitive and reward-based behavior (Baxter and Murray, 2002; Wassum and Izquierdo, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BLA has a high degree of reciprocal long-range connectivity with other brain regions.
source: The basolateral amygdala complex (BLA) is one region that has received particular attention, in large part due to its high degree of reciprocal long-range connectivity with other brain regions (Amir et al., 2018; Janak and Tye, 2015; Little and Carter, 2013; McGarry and Carter, 2017; Senn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BLA projections to different downstream regions control a range of diverse, and sometimes bidirectional, functional and behavioral phenotypes.
source: Harnessing this experimental tractability, a body of work has emerged demonstrating that BLA projections to different downstream regions control of a range of diverse, and sometimes bidirectional, functional and behavioral phenotypes (Beyeler et al., 2018; Beyeler et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; Herry et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2013; Namburi et al., 2015; Tye et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different BLA projections can emanate from different gross geographic locations.
source: Indeed, as different BLA projections can emanate from different gross geographic locations (Beyeler et al., 2018; McGarry and Carter, 2017), there exists a potential organizational substrate wherein projection target and intrinsic identity of BLA neurons might spatially covary.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High-depth scRNA-seq data was obtained for 1231 excitatory neurons.
source: After subsequent processing and sequencing (see Methods), high-depth scRNA-seq data was obtained for 1231 excitatory neurons (5.9 ± 1.2 thousand expressed genes/cell, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data obtained in the study.

claim: The scRNA-seq profiles separated into two discretely separated groups via t-SNE visualization and principal component analysis.
source: Broadly, these scRNA-seq profiles separated into two discretely separated groups via t-SNE visualization and principal component analysis, with this separation recapitulated by graph-based clustering (see Methods; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Random classifiers trained on 100 randomly selected cells achieved 91.8% +/- 3.7% accuracy in predicting classification of the remaining 1131 cells.
source: Such discrete separation was robust, as random classifiers trained on 100 randomly selected cells (~8.1% of total dataset) was sufficient to predict near-perfect classification accuracy of the remaining dataset (91.8% +/- 3.7% accuracy of remaining 1131 cells, N = 1000 trials, mean ± SD; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the random forest classification analysis.

claim: Sequenced cells expressed markers of neurons in general (e.g. Snap25).
source: Broadly, sequenced cells expressed markers of neurons in general (e.g. Snap25), as well as more specific markers of excitatory neurons (e.g. Slc17a7, encoding Vglut1, and Camk2a; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sequenced cells expressed markers of excitatory neurons (e.g. Slc17a7, encoding Vglut1, and Camk2a).
source: Broadly, sequenced cells expressed markers of neurons in general (e.g. Snap25), as well as more specific markers of excitatory neurons (e.g. Slc17a7, encoding Vglut1, and Camk2a; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expression of markers for inhibitory neurons (e.g., Gad1 and Slc32a1) was effectively absent in the sequenced cells.
source: As expected, expression of markers for inhibitory neurons (e.g., Gad1 and Slc32a1) was effectively absent.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both coarse clusters of BLA cells represented excitatory neuronal populations.
source: Thus, both coarse clusters of BLA cells represented excitatory neuronal populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of excitatory markers and absence of inhibitory markers.

claim: Excitatory subtypes of BLA cells were not resolved in a recently published relatively low-depth droplet-based scRNA-seq dataset (Zeisel et al., 2018).
source: Such excitatory subtypes of BLA cells were not resolved in a recently published relatively low-depth droplet-based scRNA-seq dataset (Zeisel et al., 2018) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2), highlighting the utility of our high-depth manual capture approach.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A total of 415 differentially expressed genes were identified between the two clusters at an adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05.
source: Using an adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05, we identified a total of 415 differentially expressed genes between the two clusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from differential expression analysis.

claim: Marker genes for cluster 1 (e.g. Negr1, Ddit4l) were generally enriched in posterior sections, occupying the lateral-dorsal regions of the BLA.
source: Marker genes for cluster 1 (e.g. Negr1, Ddit4l) were generally enriched in posterior sections, occupying the lateral-dorsal regions of the BLA (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Spatial enrichment of cluster 1 marker genes corresponds to the lateral amygdala (LA).
source: Notably, such spatial enrichment corresponds to the lateral amygdala (LA; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of marker genes and atlas definitions.

claim: Expression of marker genes for cluster 2 (e.g. Cplx1, Lynx1) was generally present in the basal amygdala (BA).
source: Conversely, expression of marker genes for cluster 2 (e.g. Cplx1, Lynx1) was generally present in the basal amygdala (BA), abutting and largely nonoverlapping with expression for cluster one markers (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Cluster 1 corresponds to the LA and cluster 2 corresponds to the BA.
source: Thus, spatial registration of cluster 1 and cluster 2 indicated that these clusters corresponded to the LA and BA, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of marker genes.

claim: The relative representation of the two clusters in the scRNA-seq dataset was similar to the relative abundance of LA and BA neurons counted from ISH.
source: Consistent with this, the relative representation of the two clusters in the scRNA-seq dataset was similar to the relative abundance of LA and BA neurons counted from ISH (scRNA-seq: 27% and 73% from LA and BA neurons respectively, cf. 39% and 61% from ISH using atlas delineation of LA vs. BA).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of the scRNA-seq and ISH data.

claim: Finer clustering split the LA into two subpopulations and the BA into four subpopulations.
source: To begin, we allowed finer clustering of our scRNA-seq dataset, which split the LA into two subpopulations and the BA into four subpopulations (Figure 4A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Subpopulations were generally abutting and/or interspersed when projections onto the first two principal components were examined.
source: Such subpopulations were generally abutting and/or interspersed when projections onto the first two principal components were examined (Figure 4B), as well as with UMAP dimensionality reduction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that these subpopulations might reflect graded differences within the LA and BA rather than discrete subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Random forest classification was relatively error-prone for the finer subpopulations, with neurons at the interface of within-LA and within-BA subpopulations being poorly classified.
source: Reinforcing this, random forest classification was relatively error-prone, with neurons that occupied the interface of within-LA and within-BA subpopulations being poorly classified in particular (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the random forest classification results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 199 genes were differentially expressed between the two LA subpopulations at padjusted <0.05.
source: We first pursued this by examining heterogeneity within the LA, leveraging the fact that gene expression between the two subpopulations varied substantially (e.g. 199 genes differentially expressed at padjusted <0.05; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from differential expression analysis.

claim: Enriched genes within a given LA subpopulation exhibited a high degree of gene-to-gene variation.
source: Enriched genes within a given subpopulation exhibited a high degree of gene-to-gene variation, wherein the extent of expression of one marker gene was a poor predictor of the extent of expression in another marker gene (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Differentially expressed genes between LA subpopulations did not exhibit a clear reciprocal boundary.
source: Moreover, when comparing between the two subpopulations, differentially expressed genes did not exhibit a clear reciprocal boundary that classically embodies discrete separation (Cembrowski and Menon, 2018; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: LA heterogeneity exists in a continuous spectrum, rather than adhering to discretely separated populations.
source: All of these observed signatures are suggestive of LA heterogeneity existing in a continuous spectrum, rather than adhering to discretely separated populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression patterns observed.

claim: 147 genes were enriched within individual BA subpopulations.
source: In a similar fashion, we considered the four BA subpopulations, examining the 147 genes that were enriched within individual subpopulations (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from differential expression analysis.

claim: Enriched genes within BA subpopulations exhibited high gene-to-gene variability and lacked reciprocal boundaries between subpopulations.
source: As with the LA, these enriched genes exhibited high gene-to-gene variability within a subpopulation, and as well lacked reciprocal boundaries between subpopulations (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: Borders between subpopulations of the BA are graded rather than discrete.
source: These findings, coupled with the fact that these subpopulations were abutting and/or interleaved in dimensionally reduced spaces (Figure 4A,B) and exhibited poor separation at interfaces (Figure 4C), suggested that borders between subpopulations of the BA were graded rather than discrete.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of gene expression patterns and clustering results.

claim: Markers for LA subpopulation one (e.g. Rorb, Myl4) were relatively enriched in the anterior and dorsal LA.
source: Markers for the two subpopulations were enriched in grossly different regions of the LA: one set of subpopulation markers (e.g. Rorb, Myl4) was relatively enriched in the anterior and dorsal LA, whereas markers for the other subpopulation (e.g. Cdh13, Otof) were relatively enriched in posterior and ventral LA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Markers for LA subpopulation two (e.g. Cdh13, Otof) were relatively enriched in posterior and ventral LA.
source: Markers for the two subpopulations were enriched in grossly different regions of the LA: one set of subpopulation markers (e.g. Rorb, Myl4) was relatively enriched in the anterior and dorsal LA, whereas markers for the other subpopulation (e.g. Cdh13, Otof) were relatively enriched in posterior and ventral LA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Strict spatial boundaries between LA subpopulation marker genes were not apparent.
source: As expected from scRNA-seq, strict spatial boundaries between subpopulation marker genes were not apparent; similarly, prominent gene-to-gene variability in spatial expression within a given subpopulation was also present.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Graded spatial variation of cell-type identity exists within the LA.
source: In sum, such results suggest graded spatial variation of cell-type identity within the LA.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of marker genes.

claim: Marker genes for BA subpopulation one were generally enriched anterior and medial.
source: Marker genes for BA subpopulation one were generally enriched anterior and medial, whereas markers for BA subpopulation two were enriched in more posterior and lateral regions of the BA.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Markers for BA subpopulation two were enriched in more posterior and lateral regions of the BA.
source: Marker genes for BA subpopulation one were generally enriched anterior and medial, whereas markers for BA subpopulation two were enriched in more posterior and lateral regions of the BA.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: BA subpopulation three was enriched medially and subpopulation four was enriched laterally.
source: Markers for BA subpopulation 3 and 4 showed spatial variation, wherein subpopulation three was enriched medially and subpopulation four was enriched laterally.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: No sharp spatial delineations were seen between BA subpopulations.
source: As with the LA, no sharp spatial delineations were seen between subpopulations, and marker genes associated with the same BA subpopulation spatially varied on a gene-to-gene basis.
evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Most enriched genes are not associated with activity dependence.
source: First, most enriched genes (Figure 4D–I) are not associated with activity dependence.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the genes identified as enriched.

claim: Genes associated with activity dependence (e.g. Bdnf, Nr4a2) exhibit different patterns of expression across cells.
source: Second, for the genes that have been associated with activity dependence (e.g. Bdnf, Nr4a2), they exhibit different patterns of expression across cells (Bdnf vs. Nr4a2: scRNA-seq: Figure 4H, ISH: Figure 5C,D; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for within-sample mFISH comparison).
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4H, 5C,D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activity-driven cell-state differences are small relative to baseline cell-type variability in the BLA.
source: Although we cannot completely discount activity states driving some gene-expression differences within the BLA population, the above results argue that activity-driven cell-state differences are small relative to baseline cell-type variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of gene expression patterns.

claim: Multiplexed single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (mFISH) mapped 12 gene-expression targets in the same tissue.
source: With this multiplexed approach, we mapped 12 gene-expression targets in the same tissue, providing a comprehensive assessment of cell-type identity and organization at single-cell resolution in space.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodology used.

claim: Phenotypes sharply transitioned across the LA-BA border.
source: Using this metric to study BLA phenotypes across space, it was apparent that phenotypes sharply transitioned across the LA-BA border (Figure 6D), with single-cell phenotypes exhibiting a bimodal distribution concentrated at extreme phenotypic index values (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the mFISH data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Single-cell phenotypes exhibited a bimodal distribution concentrated at extreme phenotypic index values.
source: Using this metric to study BLA phenotypes across space, it was apparent that phenotypes sharply transitioned across the LA-BA border (Figure 6D), with single-cell phenotypes exhibiting a bimodal distribution concentrated at extreme phenotypic index values (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the mFISH data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A spatial gradient of gene expression was identified, providing direct evidence for graded cell-type identity within BA and LA.
source: Averaging this process across all cells, we identified a spatial gradient of gene expression, providing direct evidence for graded cell-type identity within BA and LA (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by the mFISH data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Clustering of mFISH data at different resolutions recapitulated both the discrete and graded cell-type identity changes.
source: Finally, clustering of mFISH data at different resolutions recapitulated both the discrete and graded cell-type identity changes, providing further evidence of these organizational patterns within the BLA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the mFISH clustering analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: 51 interneuron single-cell transcriptomes were obtained by scRNA-seq.
source: To examine this, we next analyzed the 51 interneuron single-cell transcriptomes obtained by scRNA-seq (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data obtained.

claim: Two distinct subtypes of interneurons were identified that differentially expressed dozens of genes.
source: Despite the small number of cells in this dataset, this analysis identified two distinct subtypes of interneurons that differentially expressed dozens of genes.
evidence: This is supported by the interneuron scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Interneuron subtypes occupied distinct regions, with one subtype within the BLA and the other occupying the pericapsular region.
source: Via chromogenic ISH, we found these subtypes occupied distinct regions, with one subtype within the BLA and the other occupying the pericapsular region (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by the ISH data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: Projections to the ACX and NAC recapitulated the discrete LA-BA divide identified transcriptomically.
source: Projections to the ACX and NAC recapitulated the discrete LA-BA divide that was identified transcriptomically, such that ACX projections were enriched within the LA and NAC projections where enriched in the BA (Figure 7A–H; both obeyed p<0.001 for enrichment relative to random selected BLA neurons in N = 1000 Monte-Carlo simulations).
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7A-H.

claim: ACX projections were enriched within the LA.
source: Projections to the ACX and NAC recapitulated the discrete LA-BA divide that was identified transcriptomically, such that ACX projections were enriched within the LA and NAC projections where enriched in the BA (Figure 7A–H; both obeyed p<0.001 for enrichment relative to random selected BLA neurons in N = 1000 Monte-Carlo simulations).
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7A-H.

claim: NAC projections were enriched in the BA.
source: Projections to the ACX and NAC recapitulated the discrete LA-BA divide that was identified transcriptomically, such that ACX projections were enriched within the LA and NAC projections where enriched in the BA (Figure 7A–H; both obeyed p<0.001 for enrichment relative to random selected BLA neurons in N = 1000 Monte-Carlo simulations).
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7A-H.

claim: MEC, VHC, PFC and RSC projections were all enriched within the BA.
source: Similarly, the remaining four projections – MEC, VHC, PFC and RSC – all were enriched with the BA (Figure 7I–X; p<0.001 via N = 1000 Monte-Carlo simulations).
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7I-X.

claim: MEC, VHC, PFC and RSC projections exhibited spatially restricted regions reminiscent of BA subpopulation marker gene expression.
source: These projections furthermore exhibited spatially restricted regions reminiscent of BA subpopulation marker gene expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; p<0.001 via N = 1000 Monte-Carlo simulations when comparing to cell-to-cell distances expected by random selection of BA neurons).
evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity was present for each BLA projection examined.
source: Thus, spatial heterogeneity was present for each BLA projection examined, consistent with organizational rules observed at a transcriptomic level.
evidence: This is inferred from the retrograde tracing data.

claim: A precipitous decline in cell body size was identified for ACX-projecting neurons, relative to projections from the VHC, MEC, PFC, NAC and RSC.
source: To begin, we examined cell-body area in our projection level dataset (N = 3–5 mice per injection site, 12–82 cells/mouse). In doing so, we identified a precipitous decline in the cell body size of ACX-projecting neurons, relative to projections from the VHC, MEC, PFC, NAC and RSC (p<0.005 via Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the cell body size measurements shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: The drop in cell body size covaried with the LA vs. BA projection site of these neurons.
source: Of note, this drop covaried with the LA vs. BA projection site of these neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between cell body size and projection site.

claim: No statistical differences in cell-body size were seen for pairwise comparisons within the BA (VHC, MEC, PFC, NAC, RSC).
source: For pairwise comparisons within the BA (VHC, MEC, PFC, NAC, RSC), we saw no statistical differences in cell-body size (p>0.05 via Mann-Whitney U test for all pairwise within-BA comparisons).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical analysis results.

claim: A marked difference in cell body size exists between LA and BA excitatory neurons.
source: In doing so, we again recapitulated a marked difference in cell body size between LA and BA excitatory neurons (p<2.2×10−16 via Mann-Whitney U Test, Figure 8E), further underscoring that a discrete cell-body size difference exists between LA and BA excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the cell body size measurements from mFISH shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: The LA and BA have been partitioned with respect to histochemical stains (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) and the orientation of fibers.
source: Classically, the LA and BA have been partitioned with respect to histochemical stains (e.g. acetylcholinesterase) and the orientation of fibers (LeDoux, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: LA and BA exhibit differences in gene expression.
source: There is a variety of work that shows LA and BA also exhibit differences in gene expression (Zirlinger et al., 2001), morphology (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), and behavioral recruitment (Beyeler et al., 2018; Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LA and BA exhibit differences in morphology.
source: There is a variety of work that shows LA and BA also exhibit differences in gene expression (Zirlinger et al., 2001), morphology (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), and behavioral recruitment (Beyeler et al., 2018; Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LA and BA exhibit differences in behavioral recruitment.
source: There is a variety of work that shows LA and BA also exhibit differences in gene expression (Zirlinger et al., 2001), morphology (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), and behavioral recruitment (Beyeler et al., 2018; Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hundreds of differentially expressed genes were revealed between the LA and BA.
source: Leveraging this complete approach, our work revealed hundreds of differentially expressed genes between the LA and BA, producing discrete separation between the two nuclei in both gene-expression space and geographical space (Figures 2, 3 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq and ISH data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many differentially expressed genes between LA and BA are central to neuronal structure and function.
source: In addition to this degree of differential expression being numerically large, many of these genes were also central to neuronal structure and function, thus suggesting that higher order structural and functional differences should be apparent within the BLA.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional categories of the differentially expressed genes.

claim: Higher order structural and functional differences are apparent within the BLA.
source: This prediction was embodied by both differences in projection targets (Figure 7) and cell-body size (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the projection and morphology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Excitatory neurons of the BA vs. LA should be considered as intrinsically distinct entities.
source: Taken in concert with previous findings, this work argues that excitatory neurons of the BA vs. LA should be considered as intrinsically distinct entities (summary: Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data and previous literature.

claim: High-depth scRNA-seq data requires relatively few cells to resolve discrete subtypes.
source: In principle, discrete separation of BA subtypes may emerge with sampling additional cells; however, high-depth scRNA-seq data requires relatively few cells to resolve discrete subtypes (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3; Cembrowski et al., 2018b; Erwin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the data in the manuscript and citations to previous literature.

claim: Graded transcriptomic identity is a bona fide feature within the LA and BA.
source: Thus, this graded transcriptomic identity seems to be a bona fide feature within the LA and BA.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the scRNA-seq data.

claim: In many other brain regions, prominent graded transcriptomic heterogeneity does not have a spatial correlate.
source: Such a spatial arrangement is not necessarily expected a priori; indeed, there is evidence in many other brain regions wherein prominent graded transcriptomic heterogeneity does not have a spatial correlate (Harris et al., 2018; Stanley et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The finding of a spatial covariate of gene-expression heterogeneity facilitates histological cross-validation of scRNA-seq data.
source: The finding of a spatial covariate of this gene-expression heterogeneity is important, as it facilitates histological cross-validation of scRNA-seq data (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of scRNA-seq and ISH data.

claim: Spatial covariate of gene-expression heterogeneity provides a 'Rosetta stone' for registering and comparing work to previous spatially resolved structural and function characterizations.
source: Moreover, it provides a 'Rosetta stone' for registering and comparing our work to previous spatially resolved structural and function characterizations (Cembrowski and Spruston, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the utility of the findings.

claim: Dendritic morphologies change gradually across BLA subnuclei.
source: For example, dendritic morphologies change gradually across subnuclei (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), both the BA and LA have continua in firing patterns (Sah et al., 2003), and topographical gradients of connectivity are present across the BLA (Beyeler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both the BA and LA have continua in firing patterns.
source: For example, dendritic morphologies change gradually across subnuclei (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), both the BA and LA have continua in firing patterns (Sah et al., 2003), and topographical gradients of connectivity are present across the BLA (Beyeler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Topographical gradients of connectivity are present across the BLA.
source: For example, dendritic morphologies change gradually across subnuclei (McDonald, 1984; Sah et al., 2003), both the BA and LA have continua in firing patterns (Sah et al., 2003), and topographical gradients of connectivity are present across the BLA (Beyeler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Functional correlates are present within the BA along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Similar functional correlates, although typically sampled at a relatively coarser resolution in space, are also present within the BA along the anterior-posterior axis (Bergstrom et al., 2013; Goosens and Maren, 2001; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Graded heterogeneity may allow cell-type variability to help match the space of necessary computations in the BLA.
source: Indeed, such an organizational scheme is consistent with postulated graded representations within the BLA populations (Kyriazi et al., 2018), and thus such graded identity may allow cell-type variability to help match the space of necessary computations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed heterogeneity and previous literature.

claim: Cells that have a continuous gene-expression identity may nonetheless be functionally distinct in ways that are not predicted solely by transcriptomic organization.
source: Of particular note to the graded transcriptomic identity found here, cells that have a continuous gene-expression identity may nonetheless be functionally distinct in ways that are not predicted solely by transcriptomic organization (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A gene-expression threshold needed for associated protein products and function can effectively impose a higher-order discrete phenotype.
source: One such example of this is a gene-expression threshold needed for associated protein products and function, which can effectively impose a higher-order discrete phenotype (Cembrowski and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Magnocellular and parvocellular populations have been proposed within the BA nucleus.
source: Here, magnocellular and parvocellular populations have been proposed (Alheid, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Putative markers for magnocellular and parvocellular populations, Ppp1r1b and Rspo2, have been identified from bulk microarray analysis and associated with different behavioral recruitment and function.
source: Putative markers for these populations, Ppp1r1b and Rspo2, have been identified from bulk microarray analysis and associated with different behavioral recruitment and function (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Within the scRNA-seq data, Ppp1r1b and Rspo2 are enriched in opposite ends of the BA transcriptomic spectrum and do not conform to discrete subtypes.
source: Within our scRNA-seq data, Ppp1r1b and Rspo2 are enriched in opposite ends of the BA transcriptomic spectrum and do not conform to discrete subtypes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scRNA-seq data.

claim: Ppp1r1b and Rspo2 populations may reflect graded subtypes at a transcriptomic level, with biological nonlinearities producing apparently step-wise differences in high-order function and behavior.
source: Thus, Ppp1r1b and Rspo2 populations may reflect graded subtypes at a transcriptomic level, with biological nonlinearities producing apparently step-wise differences in high-order function and behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the scRNA-seq data and previous literature.

claim: Projections from the LA and BA have been associated with different long-range targets.
source: In previous work, projections from the LA and BA have been associated with different long-range targets (Beyeler et al., 2018; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; McGarry and Carter, 2017; Reppucci and Petrovich, 2016; Senn et al., 2014; Tsukano et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gradients that vary upon projection site have been reported at a finer spatial scale within the BA.
source: At a finer spatial scale within the BA, gradients that vary upon projection site have also been reported (Beyeler et al., 2018; McGarry and Carter, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons comprising BLA projections encompass an intrinsically diverse collection of cells.
source: Our study, revealing discrete and continuous differences in cell-type identity (Figures 2–6) that differentially map onto these long-range targets (Figure 7), shows that neurons comprising these projections encompass an intrinsically diverse collection of cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on gene expression and connectivity.

claim: Prominent heterogeneity within the BLA excitatory neuron population indicates that manipulations of different circuits target BLA neurons that can vary in intrinsic properties.
source: In particular, prominent heterogeneity within the BLA excitatory neuron population indicates that manipulations of different circuits target BLA neurons that can vary in intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed heterogeneity.

claim: Heterogeneity may make manipulation efficacy inherently variable between projections, especially for methodologies that rely on intrinsic properties of neurons to exert effects (e.g. DREADDs).
source: In principle, such heterogeneity may make manipulation efficacy inherently variable between projections, especially for methodologies that rely on intrinsic properties of neurons to exert effects (e.g. DREADDs: Roth, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The scRNA-seq data is hosted online in conjunction with analysis and visualization tools at http://scrnaseq.janelia.org/amygdala.
source: To facilitate the continued use of our data, we have hosted our scRNA-seq data online in conjunction with analysis and visualization tools (http://scrnaseq.janelia.org/amygdala).
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: The scRNA-seq dataset has 5.9 ± 1.2 thousand expressed genes per cell (mean ± SD).
source: After subsequent processing and sequencing (see Methods), high-depth scRNA-seq data was obtained for 1231 excitatory neurons (5.9 ± 1.2 thousand expressed genes/cell, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data characteristics.

claim: Cells with <10,000 total counts were excluded from analysis (n = 69 of 1370 initial cells).
source: Cells with <10,000 total counts were excluded from analysis (n = 69 of 1370 initial cells).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing steps.

claim: Putative non-neuronal cells (n = 19) were eliminated from the dataset by rejecting cells that exhibited CPM < 250 for Snap25.
source: Putative non-neuronal cells (n = 19) were eliminated from the dataset by rejecting cells that exhibited CPM < 250 for Snap25, a pan-neuronal marker.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing steps.

claim: Interneurons (n = 51) were eliminated from the excitatory neuron dataset by rejecting cells that exhibited CPM > 100 for Gad1.
source: For examining excitatory neurons (Figures 2–5), interneurons (n = 51) were eliminated from the dataset by rejecting cells that exhibited CPM > 100 for Gad1, an interneuron marker.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing steps.

claim: Variable genes (n = 108) used for PCA were obtained with Seurat.
source: Variable genes (n = 108) used for PCA were obtained with Seurat via FindVariableGenes(mean.function = ExpMean, dispersion.function = LogVMR, x.low.cutoff = 0.125, x.high.cutoff = 3, y.cutoff = 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis methods.

claim: Clusters were obtained with Seurat via FindClusters, using resolution = 0.2 to obtain two coarse discrete clusters and resolution = 0.8 to examine finer-scale heterogeneity.
source: Clusters were obtained with Seurat via FindClusters(reduction.type = 'pca', dims. use = 1:10), using resolution = 0.2 to obtain two coarse discrete clusters and resolution = 0.8 to examine finer-scale heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis methods.

claim: Subpopulation-specific enriched genes obeying pADJ < 0.05 were obtained with Seurat via FindMarkers().
source: In all cases, subpopulation-specific enriched genes obeying pADJ < 0.05 were obtained with Seurat via FindMarkers(), where is the pADJ is the adjusted p-value from Seurat based on Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis methods.

claim: t-SNE visualization used perplexity = 30 (interneuron analysis: 20), with 1000 iterations on the default seed.
source: t-SNE visualization van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008 used perplexity = 30 (interneuron analysis: 20), with 1000 iterations (sufficient for convergence) on the default seed.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis methods.

claim: UMAP visualization was obtained via the R UMAP package, using default parameters, performed on the scaled Seurat dataset with highly variable genes.
source: UMAP visualization (Becht et al., 2019) was obtained via the R UMAP package, using default parameters, performed on the scaled Seurat dataset with highly variable genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data analysis methods.

claim: Raw and processed scRNA-seq datasets have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus under GEO: GSE148866.
source: Raw and processed scRNA-seq datasets have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus under GEO: GSE148866.
